author: Jakson Gudawela
headline: Inspector availability shapes Gulf refinery turnaround scheduling
deck: The shutdown window is the most expensive period in a plant's calendar, and the constraint on it is increasingly people rather than parts.
excerpt: Gulf refinery and petrochemical turnarounds are increasingly constrained by the availability of qualified inspection personnel rather than by materials or production planning.
content:
The disciplines represented at STATIC Arabia in Al Khobar this week — inspection, integrity assessment, repair and replacement of static equipment — all converge on one event in a process plant's calendar: the turnaround.

A turnaround is a planned total shutdown during which equipment that cannot be examined while operating is opened, inspected, repaired and returned to service. It is the most expensive period in a plant's operating cycle, because the facility earns nothing while it is down and because the work is compressed into a fixed window by the cost of extending it.

The planning horizon is long, typically years, and the scope is built from a list of items requiring attention: vessels due for internal inspection, exchangers requiring tube work, columns needing tray repairs, valves and relief devices due for testing. That list is assembled from inspection history and risk-based assessment, which is why the risk-based inspection discipline matters commercially — it determines what goes on the list and what can safely wait for the next cycle.

The constraint that has tightened is personnel. A turnaround requires a large number of qualified people simultaneously: inspectors certified in the relevant techniques, welders qualified to the applicable procedures, and supervisors who have run this kind of work before. The Gulf's plants tend to schedule turnarounds in cooler months for the obvious reason that work in confined spaces in summer is dangerous and slow, which concentrates regional demand for the same specialists into the same weeks.

The result is that operators compete for inspection and specialist welding capacity, and a plant that cannot secure it may find its turnaround dictated by contractor availability rather than by its own production planning. That is the practical form of the localisation gap examined separately in this publication's coverage of non-destructive testing capability: the shortage is not of people who can weld but of people qualified to determine what needs welding.

Scope growth is the other persistent problem. Inspection during a turnaround routinely finds conditions worse than expected, which adds work to a window sized for the planned scope. Every turnaround carries contingency for this, and every turnaround manager knows the contingency is an estimate.

The mitigation the industry has pursued is to reduce what requires a shutdown at all — on-stream inspection techniques, monitoring that tracks degradation continuously, and risk-based intervals that extend the period between shutdowns where the evidence supports it. Each shifts work out of the critical window.
